newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Dixons shares dive on OFT inquiry.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Dixons shares dive on OFT inquiry.

text.p: Shares in Britain's biggest electrical retailer Dixons Group Plc dropped on Tuesday as the company came under scrutiny for alleged anti-competitive practices when it rents space in new retail parks.

Following a report in the Times newspaper, the Office of Fair Trading (OFT) confirmed it was investigating complaints that Dixons had attempted to use its market muscle to block rivals from taking space in out-of-town retail developments.
Dixons shares were down 15-1/2p or 3.1 percent at 480-1/2 by 1125 GMT.
A spokesman for the OFT said it had received a number of complaints and was seeking comment from Dixons' rivals and from property developers, before deciding whether to take any further action.

However the spokesman declined further comment on the identity of those who had complained, or on the number of complaints it had received. He said the OFT had asked for comment last month had asked for replies by May 9.
Dixons, however, responded to the Times report by saying it had "absolutely no market power" in new retail developments.
In a statement, Dixons said the market for space in new retail parks was highly competitive and each developer was free to decide to whom it lets its space and on what terms.
"Dixons, like any other retailer, is free to negotiate the terms on which it is prepared to make significant investments in these developments," the company said.
"Dixons has absolutely no market power in this market place and has to compete fiercely with all other retailers for space. We have made this position clear to the OFT."
It added that over 90 percent of all retail park outlets were in locations where competitors trade from the same park or trading area.
The latest inquiry is the latest example of Dixons coming under the scrutiny of the UK competition authorities.
The OFT said last July it was continuing to study the profitable extended warranties sold by Dixons and other electrical retailers such as Comet, a unit of Kingfisher Plc.
After a study of extended warranties, the OFT in January last year told retailers to comply with a voluntary code requiring them to display the price of warranties on offer.

The relationship between manufacturers and retailers such as Dixons and Comet is also under investigation by the Monopolies and Mergers Commission, amid criticism of the high degree of uniformity in retail prices for many electrical products.
Analysts said the latest OFT inquiry was bound to be a fresh concern for Dixons, but added that it posed no obvious immediate threat to its business.

"Dixons should be concerned if it has an OFT probe," said William Cullum, analyst at Paribas Capital Markets, "but on the other hand it's easy to imagine their response (to the OFT), that it's up to the landlord to decide what the correct mix should be in any development."
Cullum said the latest OFT inquiry added a fresh element of uncertainty around Dixons shares, which rose sharply through the past two years.
"We have been seeing a change of sentiment towards the stock and maybe people are just taking the view that a bit more uncertainty is coming into the equation," Cullum said.
